title: Seating Arrangement Basics

steps.title: Linear vs circular
steps.content: Linear arrangements place people in a row (often facing north or south). Circular arrangements place them around a table; left/right depend on facing direction. Service papers love fixed clues plus one ‘who sits second to the left’ question.
steps.tip: Draw the diagram every time. Never try to hold five positions in working memory.

steps.title: Left and right in a row
steps.content: If people face north in a single row, your left is their left when you stand behind them facing the same way. Standard exam convention: ‘A is second to the left of B’ means from the perspective of the people in the row facing you or as marked — always follow the facing direction given in the problem.
steps.example: Facing north: left is west, right is east.

steps.title: Place from a clue
steps.prompt: Five seats in a row facing north: A, B, C, D, E. B sits at one end. A sits second to the right of B. If B is at the left end, who is in the middle?
options: Cannot be determined from this alone
steps.explanation: With only B at left end and A second to B’s right, seats are B, ?, A, ?, ?. The middle seat is still unknown without more clues.
hints: Place B, then A, then see what remains open.

steps.title: Definite vs indefinite clues
steps.content: A definite clue pins a person to a unique seat (or unique relative seat). An indefinite clue leaves two or more possibilities. Good solvers mark both possibilities lightly until a later clue eliminates one.
steps.tip: Never force a unique placement when the clue still allows two cases.

steps.title: Second to the left
steps.prompt: In a row of six facing north, P is second to the left of Q. Q is not at either end. How many seats are between P and Q?
steps.explanation: ‘Second to the left’ means exactly one person sits between them on that side — so one seat between P and Q.
hints: Second to the left ≠ immediately left.
Count positions carefully on a sketch.

steps.title: Circular facing centre
steps.prompt: Eight people sit around a circular table facing the centre. Who is to the immediate left of a person?
options: Cannot define left in a circle
steps.explanation: When facing the centre, immediate left is anti-clockwise for the standard top-view diagram used in most keys.
hints: Your left hand points anti-clockwise in the usual top view.

steps.title: Catch the flawed assumption
steps.prompt: A student assumes ‘A sits between B and C’ means A is exactly in the middle of the whole row. What is wrong?
options: ‘Between B and C’ only means B and C are on either side of A (adjacent or with others, depending on wording)
Between always means ends of the row
A cannot sit between two people
The statement is never used in exams
steps.explanation: ‘Between’ is a relative clue about B, A, C — not a claim that A is the global middle unless stated.
hints: Sketch B–A–C as a block when clues say immediate between.

questions.prompt: Best first step for any seating puzzle?
options: Draw positions and mark facing direction
questions.explanation: A diagram with facing direction prevents left/right errors.

questions.prompt: ‘Second to the right’ of X means:
options: Skip one seat on X’s right
questions.explanation: Second to the right skips exactly one person/seat on that side.

questions.prompt: In a circle facing the centre, immediate right is commonly:
questions.explanation: Facing centre → immediate right is clockwise in standard top-view convention.

questions.prompt: A clue still allows two placements. You should:
options: Mark both cases until another clue decides
Place the person at an end
questions.explanation: Carry dual cases; elimination comes from later definite clues.

questions.prompt: Five in a row; A at left end; B second to the right of A. Position of B?
questions.explanation: Seats: A, _, B, _, _. B is third from the left.

learning_objectives: Draw linear and circular seating diagrams

common_misconceptions.misconception: Left and right are absolute on the page.
common_misconceptions.correction: Left and right follow the facing direction of the people.

company_applications.practice: Short linear sets with 4–5 definite clues.
Circular facing-centre with ‘who sits second to the left’.
Mixed indefinite clues requiring dual cases.

srs_cards.question: Facing centre, which way is immediate left?
srs_cards.answer: Anti-clockwise in the standard top-view diagram.

srs_cards.question: What if a clue allows two seats?
srs_cards.answer: Mark both possibilities until a later clue eliminates one.
